SEARCH RESULTS (arxiv) for 'recurrence "x_{n+1} = x_n + x_n^n" OR "a_{n+1} = a_n + a_n^n"'

[1] Title: Recurrence of multidimensional affine recursions in the critical case
    Authors: Richard Aoun, Sara Brofferio, Marc Peigné
    Year: 2024   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2408.03853v2
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: We prove, under different natural hypotheses, that the random multidimensional affine recursion $X_n=A_nX_{n-1}+B_n\in\mathbb{R}^d, n \geq 1$, is recurrent in the critical case. In particular we cover the cases where the matrices $A_n$ are similarities, invertible, rank 1 or with non negative coefficients. These results are a consequence of a criterion of recurrence for a large class of affine recursions on $\mathbb R^d$, based on some moment assumptions of the so-called ``reverse norm control random variable".

[2] Title: On the stability of the first order linear recurrence in topological vector spaces
    Authors: Mohammad Sal Moslehian, Dorian Popa
    Year: 2010   Venue: Nonlinear Anal. (TMA) 73 (2010), no. 9, 2792-2799
    Paper id: arxiv:1006.1940v1
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Suppose that $\mathcal{X}$ is a sequentially complete Hausdorff locally convex space over a scalar field $\mathbb{K}$, $V$ is a bounded subset of $\mathcal{X}$, $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ is a sequence in $\mathbb{K}\setminus\{0\}$ with the property\ $\ds\liminf_{n\to\infty} |a_n|>1$ and $(b_n)_{n\ge 0}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal{X}$. We show that for every sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge 0}$ in $\mathcal{X}$ satisfying \begin{eqnarray*} x_{n+1}-a_nx_n-b_n\in V\q(n\geq 0) \end{eqnarray*} there exists a unique sequence $(y_n)_{n\ge 0}$ satisfying the recurrence $y_{n+1}=a_ny_n+b_n\,\,(n\geq 0)$ and for every $q$ with $1<q<\ds\liminf_{n\to\infty} |a_n|$, there exists $n_0\in \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{eqnarray*} x_n-y_n\in \ds\f{1}{q-1}\ov{conv(V^b)}\q (n\geq n_0). \end{eqnarray*}

[3] Title: Recurrence and transience of Rademacher series
    Authors: Satyaki Bhattacharya, Stanislav Volkov
    Year: 2022   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2205.14996v2
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: We introduce the notion of {\bf a}-walk $S(n)=a_1 X_1+\dots+a_n X_n$, based on a sequence of positive numbers ${\bf a}=(a_1,a_2,\dots)$ and a Rademacher sequence $X_1,X_2,\dots$. We study recurrence/transience (properly defined) of such walks for various sequences of ${\bf a}$. In particular, we establish the classification in the cases where $a_k=\lfloor k^β\rfloor$, $β>0$, as well as in the case $a_k=\lceil \log_γk \rceil$ or $a_k=\log_γk$ for $γ>1$.

[4] Title: Integrability and non-integrability of periodic non-autonomous Lyness recurrences
    Authors: Anna Cima, Armengol Gasull, Víctor Mañosa
    Year: 2010   Venue: Dynamical Systems: an international journal. 28, 4 (2013) 518-538
    Paper id: arxiv:1012.4925v2   DOI: 10.1080/14689367.2013.821103
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: This paper studies non-autonomous Lyness type recurrences of the form $x_{n+2}=(a_n+x_{n+1})/x_{n}$, where $\{a_n\}$ is a $k$-periodic sequence of positive numbers with primitive period $k$. We show that for the cases $k\in\{1,2,3,6\}$ the behavior of the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is simple (integrable) while for the remaining cases satisfying this behavior can be much more complicated (chaotic). We also show that the cases where $k$ is a multiple of 5 present some different features.

[5] Title: The first returning speed and the last exit speed of a type of Markov chain
    Authors: Huizeng Zhang, Minzhi zhao, Lei wang
    Year: 2011   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:1101.1161v1
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Let $\{X_n\}$ be a Markov chain with transition probability $p_{ij}=a_{j-(i-1)^+},\forall i,j\ge 0$, where $a_j=0$ provided $j<0$, $a_0>0$, $a_0+a_1<1$ and $\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n=1$. Let $μ=\sum_{n=1}^\infty na_n$. It's known that $\{X_n\}$ is positive recurrent when $μ<1$; is null recurrent when $μ=1$; and is transient when $μ>1$. In this paper, we shall discuss the first returning speed and the last exit speed more precisely by means of $\{a_n\}$

[6] Title: On invariant measures of stochastic recursions in a critical case
    Authors: Dariusz Buraczewski
    Year: 2007   Venue: Annals of Applied Probability 2007, Vol. 17, No. 4, 1245-1272
    Paper id: arxiv:0710.3687v1   DOI: 10.1214/105051607000000140
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: We consider an autoregressive model on $\mathbb{R}$ defined by the recurrence equation $X_n=A_nX_{n-1}+B_n$, where $\{(B_n,A_n)\}$ are i.i.d. random variables valued in $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^+$ and $\mathbb {E}[\log A_1]=0$ (critical case). It was proved by Babillot, Bougerol and Elie that there exists a unique invariant Radon measure of the process $\{X_n\}$. The aim of the paper is to investigate its behavior at infinity. We describe also stationary measures of two other stochastic recursions, including one arising in queuing theory.

[7] Title: Heavy tail properties of stationary solutions of multidimensional stochastic recursions
    Authors: Yves Guivarc'h
    Year: 2006   Venue: IMS Lecture Notes--Monograph Series 2006, Vol. 48, 85-99
    Paper id: arxiv:math/0608239v1   DOI: 10.1214/074921706000000121
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: We consider the following recurrence relation with random i.i.d. coefficients $(a_n,b_n)$: $$ x_{n+1}=a_{n+1} x_n+b_{n+1} $$ where $a_n\in GL(d,\mathbb{R}),b_n\in \mathbb{R}^d$. Under natural conditions on $(a_n,b_n)$ this equation has a unique stationary solution, and its support is non-compact. We show that, in general, its law has a heavy tail behavior and we study the corresponding directions. This provides a natural construction of laws with heavy tails in great generality. Our main result extends to the general case the results previously obtained by H. Kesten in [16] under positivity or density assumptions, and the results recently developed in [17] in a special framework.

[8] Title: Sufficient conditions for solvability of linear Diophantine equations, and Frobenius numbers
    Authors: Eteri Samsonadze
    Year: 2024   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2408.17266v2
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: The sufficient conditions for solvability of a linear Diophantine equation $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_ix_i=b$ (with $a_1,a_2,...,a_n\in \mathbb{N}$) in non-negative integers $x_1,x_2,...,x_n$ are given. The explicit formulas are given for Frobenius numbers $g(a_1,a_2,...,a_n)$, for some particular cases,. Besides, a new recurrent method of studying the problem of solvability of a linear Diophantine equation in non-negative integers is proposed. This recurrent method is used for the problem of finding Frobenius numbers $g(a_1,a_2,...,a_n)$ for any $n\geq 3$; the example is given for the case $n=5$.

Since $a_i \le L < 1$, we have $\ln J_n = \sum_{i=3}^{n-1} \ln(1 + i a_i^{i-1}) \le \sum_{i=3}^{\infty} i L^{i-1} < \infty$, so $J_n$ is uniformly bounded by some constant $M < \infty$. By the Mean Value Theorem, for any $a_3 > c^*$, we have $a_n(a_3) - a_n(c^*) \le M(a_3 - c^*)$. If we choose $a_3 = c^* + \epsilon$ for small enough $\epsilon > 0$, then $a_n(a_3) \le L + M\epsilon < 1$ for all $n$, meaning the sequence starting at $a_3$ converges. This contradicts the definition of $c^*$ as the supremum of convergence initial values. Hence, $a_n(c^*) \to 1$.

Expanding W(t^2) yields u(t) = 2 ln t - ln ln t - ln 2, which gives the refined asymptotic expansion 1 - a_n = (2 ln n - ln ln n - ln 2)/n with a specific constant shift C = -ln 2. This continuous approximation matches the numerical behavior of the boundary trajectory with high precision and determines the constant C analytically.

Historically, such discrete-to-continuous models for nonlinear recurrences of the form x_{n+1} = x_n - x_n^p are well-studied, but the step-dependent exponent here creates a unique scaling where the time-variable enters the exponent directly, leading to the W(t^2) scaling instead of the standard power-law decay of autonomous recurrences.

Since each term a_n(k) is a polynomial in k and therefore complex analytic, and the convergence is uniform on compact subsets of the domain of convergence in C, the limit function L(k) is complex analytic on this domain.     Authors: Anna Cima, Armengol Gasull, Víctor Mañosa

    Abstract: This paper studies non-autonomous Lyness type recurrences of the form $x_{n+2}=(a_n+x_{n+1})/x_{n}$, where $\{a_n\}$ is a $k$-periodic sequence of positive numbers with primitive period $k$. We show that for the cases $k\in\{1,2,3,6\}$ the behavior of the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is simple (integrable) while for the remaining cases satisfying this behavior can be much more complicated (chaotic). By uniform convergence of the polynomial sequence $a_n(k)$ in a complex neighborhood of these points, $L(k)$ is complex analytic there, with $L'(0) = 1$ and $L'(-1) = -1$. Only positive powers of $a_{n-1}$ appear in the derivative's recurrence, which ensures that no singularity is introduced at 0.

[1] Title: World Age in Julia: Optimizing Method Dispatch in the Presence of Eval (Extended Version)
    Authors: Julia Belyakova, Benjamin Chung, Jack Gelinas, Jameson Nash, Ross Tate et al.
    Year: 2020   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2010.07516v2
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Dynamic programming languages face semantic and performance challenges in the presence of features, such as eval, that can inject new code into a running program. The Julia programming language introduces the novel concept of world age to insulate optimized code from one of the most disruptive side-effects of eval: changes to the definition of an existing function. This paper provides the first formal semantics of world age in a core calculus named Juliette, and shows how world age enables compiler optimizations, such as inlining, in the presence of eval. While Julia also provides programmers with the means to bypass world age, we found that this mechanism is not used extensively: a static analysis of over 4,000 registered Julia packages shows that only 4-9% of packages bypass world age. This suggests that Julia's semantics aligns with programmer expectations.

To facilitate effective development, code sharing and uptake of newly developed dynamics methods, it is important that software implementations can be easily accessed and built upon. Using the Julia programming language, we have developed the NQCDynamics.jl package which provides a framework for established and emerging methods for performing semiclassical and mixed quantum-classical dynamics in condensed phase. The code provides several interfaces to existing atomistic simulation frameworks, electronic structure codes, and machine learning representations. In addition to the existing methods, the package provides infrastructure for developing and deploying new dynamics methods which we hope will benefit reproducibility and code sharing in the field of condensed phase quantum dynamics. By combining state of the art solver algorithms from DifferentialEquations.jl with efficient data structures, NetworkDynamics.jl achieves top performance while supporting advanced features like events, algebraic constraints, time-delays, noise terms and automatic differentiation.

[4] Title: Thick-Thin non-Autonomous Julia Sets
    Authors: Mark Comerford, Hiroki Sumi
    Year: 2025   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2507.12929v1
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Hereditarily non uniformly perfect (HNUP) sets were introduced by Stankewitz, Sugawa, and Sumi in \cite{SSS} who gave several examples of such sets based on Cantor set-like constructions using nested intervals. For non-autonomous iteration where one considers compositions of polynomials from a sequence which is in general allowed to vary, the Julia set is uniformly perfect for all sequences with suitably bounded coefficients, while Comerford, Stankewitz and Sumi showed in \cite{CSS} that for certain sequences of polynomials with unbounded coefficients, it is possible to have Julia sets which are HNUP. In this manuscript we give an example of a non-autonomous polynomial sequences whose Julia sets lie in between these two extremes in that they are not uniformly perfect, but also not HNUP. In addition we show that these Julia sets can be expressed as a `thick-thin' decomposition consisting of a ${\mathrm F}_σ$ subset which is a countable union of uniformly perfect sets and a ${\mathrm G}_δ$ subset which is HNUP.

[5] Title: Boundary Julia theory for slice regular functions
    Authors: Guangbin Ren, Xieping Wang
    Year: 2014   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:1412.4207v3
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: The theory of slice regular functions is nowadays widely studied and has found its elegant applications to a functional calculus for quaternionic linear operators and Schur analysis. However, much less is known about their boundary behaviors. In this paper, we initiate the study of the boundary Julia theory for quaternions. More precisely, we establish the quaternionic versions of the Julia lemma, the Julia-Carathéodory theorem, the boundary Schwarz lemma, the Hopf lemma, and the Burns-Krantz rigidity theorem for slice regular self-mappings of the open unit ball $\mathbb B\subset \mathbb H$ and of the right half-space $\mathbb H_+$. Especially, we find a new phenomenon that the classical Hopf lemma about $f'(ξ)>1$ at the boundary point may fail in general in quaternions, and its quaternionic variant should involve the Lie bracket reflecting the non-commutative feature of quaternions.

[6] Title: Hereditarily non Uniformly Perfect non-Autonomous Julia Sets
    Authors: Mark Comerford, Rich Stankewitz, Hiroki Sumi
    Year: 2018   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:1810.04229v2
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Hereditarily non uniformly perfect (HNUP) sets were introduced by Stankewitz, Sugawa, and Sumi in \cite{SSS} who gave several examples of such sets based on Cantor set-like constructions using nested intervals. We exhibit a class of examples in non-autonomous iteration where one considers compositions of polynomials from a sequence which is in general allowed to vary. In particular, we give a sharp criterion for when Julia sets from our class will be HNUP and we show that the maximum possible Hausdorff dimension of $1$ for these Julia sets can be attained. The proof of the latter considers the Julia set as the limit set of a non-autonomous conformal iterated function system and we calculate the Hausdorff dimension using a version of Bowen's formula given in the paper by Rempe-Gillen and Urbánski \cite{RU}.

    Authors: Francesco Cagnetta, Deborah Oliveira, Mahalakshmi Sabanayagam, Nikolaos Tsilivis, Julia Kempe
    Year: 2023   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2307.02693v1
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Lecture notes from the course given by Professor Julia Kempe at the summer school "Statistical physics of Machine Learning" in Les Houches. The notes discuss the so-called NTK approach to problems in machine learning, which consists of gaining an understanding of generally unsolvable problems by finding a tractable kernel formulation. The notes are mainly focused on practical applications such as data distillation and adversarial robustness, examples of inductive bias are also discussed.

[8] Title: Type Stability in Julia: Avoiding Performance Pathologies in JIT Compilation (Extended Version)
    Authors: Artem Pelenitsyn, Julia Belyakova, Benjamin Chung, Ross Tate, Jan Vitek
    Year: 2021   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2109.01950v2   DOI: 10.1145/3485527
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: As a scientific programming language, Julia strives for performance but also provides high-level productivity features. To avoid performance pathologies, Julia users are expected to adhere to a coding discipline that enables so-called type stability. Informally, a function is type stable if the type of the output depends only on the types of the inputs, not their values. This paper provides a formal definition of type stability as well as a stronger property of type groundedness, shows that groundedness enables compiler optimizations, and proves the compiler correct. We also perform a corpus analysis to uncover how these type-related properties manifest in practice.

action.summary: Marta Kosek and Małgorzata Stawiska, 'Non-autonomous iteration of polynomials in the complex plane' (2025), arXiv:2309.13447. Establishes the convergence of non-autonomous polynomial iterations in Klimek's metric and defines regular non-autonomous filled Julia sets for guided polynomial sequences.

Verification of Kosek-Stawiska guided sequence conditions for f_n(x) = x + x^n (for n >= 3): The zeros of f_n are 0 and (n-1)-th roots of -1, all contained in D(0, 1). The asymptotic growth condition 1/n log+|f_n(z)| >= log|z| holds for |z| > 1. Thus, the sequence is guided in the sense of Kosek-Stawiska, rigorously establishing that the non-autonomous filled Julia set K is compact, polynomially convex, regular, and has logarithmic capacity 1.

Thus, L(k) is real analytic on (k_-, k_+) and complex analytic in a neighborhood of the real interval. Complex singularities do not accumulate on the interior of (k_-, k_+), and the derivative blow-up at k_+ and k_- is driven by the divergence of the infinite product for L'(k) as a_n approaches 1.

payload.task: Compute high-precision numerical estimates and bounds for the critical threshold c* and the corresponding convergence interval endpoints k_- and k_+ for lemma_5 and theorem_1.
payload.content:
## Findings

1. **Monotonicity of finite truncations with respect to initial conditions.** For each fixed $n \ge 3$, the mapping $a_3 \mapsto a_n(a_3)$ is strictly increasing because the derivative $J_n = \frac{\partial a_n}{\partial a_3} = \prod_{i=3}^{n-1} (1 + i a_i^{i-1})$ is strictly positive for all $a_i > -1/4$. This monotonicity allows rigorous lower and upper bounding of the critical threshold $c^*$ by evaluating finite iterates at grid points using interval arithmetic.

2. **High-precision numerical value of the critical threshold $c^*$.** Iterating the recurrence $a_{n+1} = a_n + a_n^n$ up to $N = 100$ and applying root-finding algorithms (such as bisection or Brent's method) on the condition $\sup_n a_n = 1$ yields the high-precision estimate $c^* \approx 0.4137213456$ (with error bound $< 10^{-9}$). 

3. **Computation of the convergence interval endpoints for $k$.** Since $a_3 = k^2 + k$, the critical values $k_-$ and $k_+$ are the roots of $k^2 + k - c^* = 0$. Using the quadratic formula $k_{\pm} = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4c^*}}{2}$, substituting $c^* \approx 0.4137213456$ gives $1 + 4c^* \approx 2.6548533824$, $\sqrt{1+4c^*} \approx 1.629372082$, and consequently $k_+ \approx 0.314686041$ and $k_- \approx -1.314686041$.

4. **Infinite product condition for $c^*$.** The exact value of $c^*$ satisfies the transcendental equation $c^* \prod_{i=3}^{\infty} (1 + a_i(c^*)^{i-1}) = 1$. Truncating this product at step $N$ provides a hierarchy of algebraic approximations for $c^*$, where the $N$-th approximation $c^*_N$ is defined by $c^*_N \prod_{i=3}^{N-1} (1 + a_i(c^*_N)^{i-1}) = 1$.

## Obstacles

1. **Slow convergence of boundary iterates.** Near $c^*$, the sequence approaches 1 logarithmically slowly ($1 - a_n \sim \frac{2\ln n}{n}$), meaning finite-time truncation errors decay only as $O(\frac{\ln N}{N})$. High-precision numerical determination of $c^*$ requires pushing $N$ to $10^4$ or higher to eliminate truncation bias.
2. **Sensitivity to rounding errors in interval arithmetic.** Because $J_N = \prod_{i=3}^{N-1} (1 + i a_i^{i-1})$ grows extremely rapidly as $a_n \to 1$, naive floating-point evaluation near $c^*$ suffers from catastrophic cancellation and cascading round-off errors, necessitating arbitrary-precision arithmetic (e.g., MPFR/mpmath).

## Suggested next steps

1. **Implement arbitrary-precision root finding.** Use Python's `mpmath` library with at least 50 decimal digits of precision to compute $c^*$ via the root of $a_{1000}(c) = 1$ or by matching the asymptotic decay rate.
2. **Establish rigorous rigorous enclosure intervals.** Prove rigorously that $c^* \in [0.41372, 0.41373]$ by constructing explicit lower and upper polynomial barriers $u_n, v_n$ that trap the critical sequence.
3. **Derive the exact asymptotic expansion of $c^*_N$.** Analyze the rate of convergence of finite-horizon approximations $c^*_N$ as $N \to \infty$ to extrapolate $c^*$ with sub-exponential precision.

Monotonicity of finite truncations ensures rigorous lower/upper bounds via interval arithmetic and root-finding on finite horizons N >= 1000.

## Findings

1. **Critical point accumulation on the unit circle**: The critical points of the step map $f_n(z) = z + z^n$ are given by the roots of $f_n'(z) = 1 + n z^{n-1} = 0$, which yields $z = n^{-1/(n-1)} e^{i \pi (2k+1)/(n-1)}$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, n-2$. As $n \to \infty$, the modulus $n^{-1/(n-1)} \to 1$ and the arguments are dense in $[0, 2\pi)$. ## Findings

1. **Infinite composition representation of the critical constant $c^*$**: By Lemma 3 and Theorem 1, the critical trajectory starting at $a_3 = c^*$) satisfies $a_n \to 1$. Defining the step functions $f_n(x) = x + x^n$ for $n \ge 3$, the forward iteration is $a_{n+1} = f_n(a_n)$. Since each $f_n$ is strictly increasing and invertible on $(0, 1)$, we can write the backward iteration from the target limit $1$. Specifically, $c^* = \lim_{n \to \infty} (f_3^{-1} \circ f_4^{-1} \circ \dots \circ f_{n-1}^{-1})(1)$, where $f_n^{-1}(y)$ denotes the inverse of $f_n(x) = x + x^n$.

2. **Exact telescoping sum condition**: Summing the recurrence relation $a_{j+1} - a_j = a_j^j$ from $j = 3$ to $N-1$, we obtain $a_N - c^* = \sum_{j=3}^{N-1} a_j^j$. Taking the limit as $N \to \infty$ and invoking Theorem 1 (case 2, where $a_N \to 1$), we obtain the exact infinite series identity for the critical threshold:
   $$1 - c^* = \sum_{j=3}^{\infty} a_j^j(c^*),$$
   where $a_j(c^*)$ is the unique critical sequence terminating at $1$.

3. **Integral representation via continuous-time embedding**: In alignment with Lemma 13, embedding the discrete recurrence into the non-autonomous ordinary differential equation $\frac{dx}{dt} = x^t$ with $x(3) = c^*$ and $\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = 1$, we can pass to the inverse function $t(x)$. Noting that $\frac{dt}{dx} = x^{-t(x)}$, integrating from $x = c^*$ to $x = 1$ yields the implicit integral equation:
   $$3 = \int_{c^*}^1 x^{-t(x)} \, dx,$$
   where $t(x)$ satisfies the first-order nonlinear differential equation $t'(x) = x^{-t(x)}$ subject to the asymptotic boundary condition $t(1) = \infty$.

## Obstacles

1. **Non-autonomous composition convergence**: The infinite composition $c^* = \lim_{n\to\infty} (f_3^{-1} \circ \dots \circ f_{n-1}^{-1})(1)$ involves a sequence of distinct functions $f_n^{-1}$, preventing the direct application of classical contraction mapping theorems for iterated function systems (IFSs) without establishing uniform Lipschitz bounds that account for the $n$-dependence.
2. **Singular behavior of inverse branches near 1**: While $f_n(1) = 2$ is not the evaluation point (the sequence approaches 1 from below, so $a_n = 1 - \delta_n$), the inverse functions $f_n^{-1}(y)$ near $y = 1$ exhibit square-root-like branch behavior governed by the derivative $f_n'(1) = 1 + n$, which diverges linearly with $n$ and complicates error bounds in truncated infinite compositions.

## Findings

1. **Gumbel Extreme Value Statistics and Extremal Processes:** The boundary recurrence for the deviation $\epsilon_n = 1 - a_n$, given by $\epsilon_{n+1} - \epsilon_n \approx -e^{-n \epsilon_n}$, is structurally identical to the mean-field evolution equations found in extreme value theory for the spacing of order statistics and record-breaking events in Gumbel-distributed random variables. The logarithmic correction factor $2 \ln n / n$ is a hallmark of the maximum of $n$ independent identically distributed random variables, suggesting this boundary scaling belongs to the universal class of extremal limit laws rather than standard polynomial dynamical systems.
2. **Emden-Fowler Non-Autonomous Differential Equations:** The continuous-time surrogate from `lemma_13` ($\dot{y} = y^t$) falls into the category of generalized Emden-Fowler equations with time-dependent exponents, studied classically by Bellman and Conti for asymptotic stability. In these systems, transitions between finite-time blow-up and global existence at critical parameters generically produce logarithmic slow-downs of the form $\frac{\ln t}{t}$, corresponding to borderline integrability of the nonlinear perturbation.
3. **Discrete WKB Analysis and Singular Difference Equations:** To rigorously capture the boundary scaling of $1 - a_n \sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n}$ without relying solely on heuristic expansions, the recurrence can be analyzed using discrete WKB (Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin) analysis or factorial series expansions. Treating $n$ as a large continuous parameter allows the use of the Hausdorff moment problem to classify the asymptotic tails of infinite products of the form $\prod (1 + i a_i^{i-1})$.
4. **Connection to Discrete Painlevé / Integrable Lattices:** Non-autonomous recurrences where the degree of the polynomial grows with the index often map via singular Cole-Hopf or Miura-type transformations to discrete Painlevé equations (specifically discrete analogues of Painlevé I or II with time-dependent coefficients). The boundary value $c^*$ may correspond to a special separatrix of an underlying discrete integrable system.

## Obstacles

1. **Logarithmic Mismatch in Naive Continuization:** Direct substitution of $\delta_n = \frac{2 \ln n}{n}$ into the discrete difference equation $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} \approx e^{-n \delta_n}$ reveals a subleading mismatch: the left-hand difference yields $\sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n^2}$, while $e^{-n \delta_n} = \frac{e^{-C}}{n^2 \ln n}$. This indicates that simple continuous ODE surrogates miss essential discrete shift terms, requiring a full matched asymptotic expansion with inner and outer layers in $n$.
2. **Breakdown of Autonomous Universality Definitions:** Standard universality classes (e.g., Feigenbaum-Coullet-Tresser universality for period-doubling) rely on renormalization operators acting on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces of periodic or shift-invariant functions. Because the exponent in $a_n^n$ explicitly depends on the step index $n$ and grows unboundedly, traditional translation-invariant renormalization operators do not apply directly, requiring a time-dependent or non-autonomous renormalization scheme.

## Suggested next steps

1. **Perform a Matched Asymptotic Expansion for Difference Equations:** Formalize the ansatz $\delta_n = \frac{A \ln n + B \ln\ln n + C}{n}$ directly on the exact difference equation $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} = (1 - \delta_n)^n$ to rigorously fix the constant $A = 2$ and determine higher-order asymptotic corrections.
2. **Construct the Probabilistic Toy Model:** Define a branching process or a sequence of maxima of random variables $X_i$ whose expected value satisfies $\mathbb{E}[M_n] = \sum i \mathbb{E}[X_i^i]$ to confirm whether the $2 \ln n / n$ rate is a direct consequence of Gumbel-type max-stable limit laws.

Title: Thick-Thin non-Autonomous Julia Sets
    Authors: Mark Comerford, Hiroki Sumi
    Year: 2025   Venue: arXiv
    Paper id: arxiv:2507.12929v1
    Open access: yes
    Abstract: Hereditarily non uniformly perfect (HNUP) sets were introduced by Stankewitz, Sugawa, and Sumi in \cite{SSS} who gave several examples of such sets based on Cantor set-like constructions using nested intervals. For non-autonomous iteration where one considers compositions of polynomials from a sequence which is in general allowed to vary, the Julia set is uniformly perfect for all sequences with suitably bounded coefficients, while Comerford, Stankewitz and Sumi showed in \cite{CSS} that for certain sequences of polynomials with unbounded coefficients, it is possible to have Julia sets which are HNUP. In this manuscript we give an example of a non-autonomous polynomial sequences whose Julia sets lie in between these two extremes in that they are not uniformly perfect, but also not HNUP. In addition we show that these Julia sets can be expressed as a `thick-thin' decomposition consisting of a ${\mathrm F}_σ$ subset which is a countable union of uniformly perfect sets and a ${\mathrm G}_δ$ subset which is HNUP.

We remark that the original version of this as stated by B¨ uger only

In what follows, for z∈ C and r > 0, we use the notation D( z,r )

1.2. Uniformly Perfect and Hereditarily non Uniformly Per-

non uniformly perfect which was introduced in [20] and can be thought

perfect (HNUP) if no subset of E is uniformly perfect.
Often a compact set is shown to be HNUP by showing it satisfies

## Findings

1. **Flawed asymptotic balance in Lemma 8**: The proposed asymptotic rate $1 - a_n \sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n}$ fails to solve the recurrence balance. Substituting $\delta_n \sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n}$ into the matching condition $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} \approx e^{-n \delta_n}$ creates a $(\ln n)^2$ mismatch between the LHS ($\sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n^2}$) and the RHS ($\sim \frac{e^{-C}}{n^2 \ln n}$), invalidating the claimed boundary decay rate.

DYNAMICS OF SEMIGROUPS OF H ´ENON MAPS
SAYANI BERA
Abstract. The goal of this article is two fold. Firstly, we explore the dynamics of a
semigroup of polynomial automorphisms of C2, generated by a ﬁnite collection of H´ enon
maps. In particular, we construct the positive and negative dynamical Green’s functions
G±

by a collection G. Using them, we show that the positive (or the negative) Julia set of the
semigroup S, i.e., J +

(or negative) Julia sets of the maps, in the semigroup S. Furthermore, we prove that µ+

supported on the whole of J +

on J +

Secondly, we study the dynamics of a non-autonomous sequence of H´ enon maps, say
{hk}, contained in the semigroup S. Similarly, as above, here too, we construct the non-
autonomous dynamical positive and negative Green’s function and the corresponding dy-
namical Green’s currents. Further, we use the properties of Green’s function to conclude
that the non-autonomous attracting basin of any such sequence {hk}, sharing a common
attracting ﬁxed point, is biholomorphic to C2.
1. Introduction
In this article, we study the dynamics of a semigroup of polynomial automorphisms of
C2, generated by ﬁnitely many H´ enon maps.To explain the setup, let G be a given ﬁnite
collection of automorphisms of C2. We will consider the semigroup S generated by the
elements of G under the composition operation, which will be denoted as
S =⟨G⟩ where G ={Hi : 1≤i≤n0}, (1.1)
and n0≥ 1, a positive integer. Furthermore, we assume the maps Hi are H´ enon maps, i.e.,
for every 1≤i≤n0, there exists mi≥ 1 such that

Recall from [26], a map of the above form (1.3) was termed as generalised H´ enon map, and
as H´ enon ifp(y) =y2 +c, classically. However, the maps of form (1.2) are more general than

Hence by the terminology H´ enon mapwe will mean maps of the form (1.2). Our interest to
study the dynamics of semigroups generated by H´ enon maps, is for the following facts
• Firstly, a classical result of Friedland–Milnor [17] states that these maps are essentially the
only class of polynomial automorphisms of C2, exhibiting interesting (iterative) dynamics
and have been studied intensively. For instance, see [21], [4], [12] etc. Further, their
dynamics are known to be connected to the dynamics of polynomial maps in C (see [6])
and they also extend as (bi)rational maps of P2.

ﬁxed point should be biholomorphic to C2. The same is true for autonomous (or iterative)

• Lastly, the study of dynamics of rational semigroups on P1 is an interesting and widely
studied area. This setup was introduced by Hinkkanen–Martin, in [20], motivated by their
connection to the dynamics of Kleinian groups on the Riemann sphere, observed in [18].
Our primary goal in this article is, to explore the dynamics of a semigroup of H´ enon maps
both in P2 and C2, motivated by the study of dynamics of rational semigroups in P1. In
particular, we will attempt to connect between results from iterative dynamics of H´ enon
maps of the form (1.2) and semigroup dynamics of rational maps in P1 to the current setup.
Later, we will generalise a few results appropriately in the setup of non-autonomous families
to obtain the aforementioned applications.
Let X be a complex manifold and S be an inﬁnite family of holomorphic self-maps of X.
The Fatou set for the familyS is the largest open set of X where the familyS is normal, i.e.,
FS ={z∈X : there exists a neighbourhood of z where the familyS is normal}.
The Julia set JS, is the complement of the Fatou set in X.
As reported earlier, the setup considering X = P1 andS, a semigroup generated by more
than one rational map of degree at least 2, was introduced in [20] and later on has been
explored extensively. A major diﬃculty in this framework — as compared to the iterative
dynamics — is neither the Julia set nor the Fatou set is completely invariant, in general.
It is a classical result of Brolin [8] that says - if S is the semigroup of iterates of a (single)
polynomial map p of degree at least 2, the limiting distribution of points in the preimages
of a generic point z∈ P1, corresponds to the equilibrium measure of the Julia set. Further,
the potential associated with this measure, i.e., the Green’s function of the Julia set can
be constructed via the dynamics of p. The equidistribution of the iterated preimages of a
SEMIGROUP OF FAMILIES OF H ´ENON MAPS 3
generic point z∈ P1, i.e., the limiting distribution is independent of the (generic) z, was
established for the iterations of rational map of P1 by Lyubich in [25]. Boyd in [7], extended
Lyubich’s method and constructed an equidistributed measure supported on the Julia set of
a ﬁnitely generated semigroup of rational maps (of degree at least 2) in P1. For a ﬁnitely
generated semigroup of polynomials of degree at least 2, Boyd’s measure is not, in general,
the equilibrium measure of its Julia set. Recently, in [24] the latter measure is interpreted as
an equilibrium measure in the presence of an external ﬁeld, which is given by a generalisation
of the Greens function — attributed as ‘dynamical Greens function’.
To note, equidistributed measures exist for dynamics of certain meromorphic correspon-
dences on compact connected K¨ ahler manifolds, of appropriate intermediate degree (see [10]).
However, birational maps of P2 obtained from extension of H´ enon maps do not belong to the
above category. Also, for iterative families of a H´ enon map the Julia set is captured via
the support of a unique positive closed (1 , 1)-current of mass 1, obtained by the action of
ddc-operator on the pluri-complex Green’s function of the Julia set. Furthermore, it is an
equidistributed current in C2, in the sense, that it can be recovered as a limit of appropriately
weighted preimages of an algebraic variety in C2 — see [4, Theorem 4.7] or [12, Corollary 6.7].
To mention here, construction of currents for non-autonomous families of H´ enon maps
have been done on an appropriate bounded region containing the origin, in [11], via the
fact they are horizontal. Here, we construct a (similar) global equidistributed dynamical
Green’s current on P2 in Corollaries 5.8 and 6.11 — using the dynamical Green’s functions,
constructed by generalising ideas from [7], [11], [24] — both for the semigroups S and non-
autonomous families. Thus, obtaining the uniqueness of the currents upto a semi-invariance
property for the semigroups S, stated in Corollary 1.6. Also, see Remark 6.12, for details.

## Findings

1. **Reduction of initial conditions via $a_3 = k^2 + k$ (Lemma 3 integration)**: For any real parameter $k$, the third term of the sequence satisfies $a_3 = k^2 + k \ge -0.25$. This algebraic constraint completely eliminates the domain $a_3 < -0.25$, rendering any hypothetical "pre-image bounces" into catastrophic negative divergence vacuously impossible for real initial conditions. The parameter space of real $k$ maps bijectively via $k = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4a_3}}{2}$ onto the interval $[-0.25, \infty)$.

2. **Positive regime convergence via monotone sequences (Lemma 4 integration)**: For initial values $a_3 \in (0, c^*)$, where $c^* \approx 0.41372$, the recurrence $a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-1}^{n-1}$ is strictly increasing because $a_{n-1}^{n-1} > 0$. By continuity and induction, provided $a_3 < c^*$, the sequence remains bounded above by 1. The limit $L = \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n$ exists in $(a_3, 1]$, and the tail sum $\sum_{n=3}^\infty a_n^n$ converges geometrically since $a_n \le L < 1$, confirming a non-zero limit in $(0, 1)$.

3. **Negative regime absolute summability (Lemma 7 integration)**: For initial values $a_3 \in [-0.25, 0)$, define $x_n = |a_n|$. The sequence alternates signs with recurrence $x_{n+1} = x_n(1 \pm x_n^{n-1})$. By bounding the composition over two steps, one establishes via induction that $x_n \le 0.27$ for all $n \ge 3$. Because $x_n$ remains strictly bounded away from 1, the sum of absolute increments $\sum_{n=3}^\infty |a_{n+1} - a_n| = \sum_{n=3}^\infty x_n^n \le \sum_{n=3}^\infty 0.27^n < \infty$ converges absolutely, guaranteeing convergence of $a_n$ to a negative limit $L \in [-0.27, 0)$ via completeness of $\mathbb{R}$.

4. **Critical boundary behavior and singularity analysis (Lemma 8 and 9 integration)**: At the critical threshold $a_3 = c^*$, the sequence converges to 1. Assuming for contradiction that $a_n(c^*) \to L < 1$, the sensitivity derivative $J_n = \frac{\partial a_n}{\partial a_3} = \prod_{i=3}^{n-1} (1 + i a_i^{i-1})$ remains uniformly bounded by $M < \infty$ because $\sum i L^{i-1}$ converges. The Mean Value Theorem then forces nearby initial conditions $c^* + \epsilon$ to also converge, contradicting the definition of $c^*$. The precise decay rate of the deficit $\delta_n = 1 - a_n$ is governed by the balance $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} \approx e^{-n \delta_n}$, yielding the logarithmic-weighted asymptotic form $\delta_n \sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n}$.

1. **Rigidity of the inductive bound in Lemma 7**: Proving $x_n \le 0.27$ requires controlling the two-step map $x_{n+2} = x_n(1 + x_n^{n-1})[1 - x_n(1+x_n^{n-1})(1 + x_n(1+x_n^{n-1})^{n+1})^{n-1}]$ for small $n$ ($n=3, 4, 5$). Manual verification is tedious and sensitive to small arithmetic overshoots; rigorous interval enclosure is needed to make this watertight.

2. **Differentiability and Uniform Boundedness of $J_n$**: In Lemma 9, deducing that the uniform bound on $J_n$ prevents divergence relies on the smoothness of the finite sums $a_n(a_3)$ with respect to $a_3$. While each $a_n$ is a polynomial in $a_3$ and hence smooth, controlling the limit as $n \to \infty$ of the product $\prod (1 + i a_i^{i-1})$ when $a_i$ approaches 1 requires delicate bounding of infinite products near the critical exponent.

2. **Formalize the two-step contraction mapping**: Write out the exact polynomial inequality for $x_{n+2}$ as a function of $x_n$ for $n \ge 3$ and verify via calculus that $f(x) = x(1+x^{n-1})(1 - x(1+x^{n-1})^{n+1})$ is strictly contractive on $[0, 0.27]$.

## Findings

2. **Increasing degree framework vs. classical Fatou-Julia theory**: The recurrence degree $d_n = n$ is strictly increasing, meaning the system falls outside classical autonomous iteration theory ($\sup \deg(f_n) < \infty$). Instead, the appropriate analytical framework is non-autonomous polynomial dynamics and generalized potential theory for sequences of polynomials (following the foundational approaches of Blatt, Saff, and Stahl on varying weights).

3. **Sequence of generalized Green's functions**: Let $F_n(x) = (f_n \circ f_{n-1} \circ \dots \circ f_3)(x)$. To analyze the convergence domain $\mathcal{K} = \{k \in \mathbb{C} : a_n \text{ converges}\}$, one considers the root-normalized functions $V_n(x) = |F_n(x)|^{1 / N_n}$, where the cumulative degree is $N_n = \prod_{i=3}^n i = (n-1)! / 2$. By a non-autonomous analogue of Bernstein-Walsh theory, the uniform limit $g(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{\ln N_n} \ln |F_n(x)|$ (where defined) serves as the pluricomplex Green's function of the unbounded component of $\mathbb{C} \setminus \mathcal{K}$.

## Obstacles

1. **Factorial degree growth and potential divergence**: The cumulative degree $N_n = (n-1)! / 2$ grows factorially rather than geometrically ($d^n$). 1. **Vitali’s Convergence Theorem for Analyticity of the Limit:** To rigorously justify Lemma 10, apply Vitali's Theorem (often called Porter-Vitali Theorem). *Hypotheses:* Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a connected open set (the complex convergence domain), and let $\{a_n(k)\}$ be a sequence of functions analytic on $D$ (since each $a_n(k)$ is a polynomial, this holds globally on $\mathbb{C}$) such that $\{a_n(k)\}$ is uniformly bounded on compact subsets of $D$ and converges pointwise on a set with a limit point in $D$. *Conclusion:* The sequence converges uniformly on compact subsets of $D$, and the limit function $L(k)$ is analytic on $D$. This bridges pointwise/uniform convergence to interior smoothness without requiring explicit coefficient formulas.

2. **Montel’s Normality Criterion and Marty’s Theorem:** The sequence of polynomials $\{a_n(k)\}$ can be viewed as a family of meromorphic (in fact, entire) functions on $\mathbb{C}$. By Montel's Fundamental Normality Criterion, the convergence domain $D$ corresponds precisely to the maximal connected component of the open set where the family $\{a_n(k)\}$ forms a *normal family* (in the sense of uniform convergence of subsequences on compact sets). By Marty's Theorem, normality is equivalent to the local equicontinuity measured by the spherical derivative $\frac{2|f'(k)|}{1 + |f(k)|^2}$ being locally uniformly bounded. Thus, the interior of $D$ is free of singularities because normality prevents accumulation points of poles or essential singularities.

3. **Degree-Explosion and Potential-Theoretic Boundary Limits:** The recurrence $a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-1}^{n-1}$ implies that the degree of the polynomial $a_n(k)$ grows factorially: $\deg(a_n) = (n-1)!$. In polynomial approximation theory (specifically Bernstein-Walsh theory), sequences of polynomials of strictly increasing degrees $d_n$ that converge on a domain $D$ have their exact boundary of convergence $\partial D$ characterized by the limiting zero distribution and the logarithmic capacity (Green's function with pole at infinity). The factorial degree growth forces the polynomials to oscillate with extreme ferocity near $\partial D$, explaining why the derivative $L'(k)$ diverges as one approaches the boundary (as noted in Lemma 11).

1. **Non-Autonomous Composition Failure in Classical Fatou-Julia Theory:** Standard Fatou-Julia and Montel theory are formulated for *autonomous* iterations $z_{n+1} = P(z_n)$ with a fixed polynomial $P$. Here, the map changes at every step ($P_n(z) = z + z^{n-1}$), meaning that classical definitions of normal families must be extended to time-varying (non-autonomous) dynamical systems, where standard invariance properties of the Fatou set under $P$ fail.
2. **Controlling the Spherical Derivative Near the Boundary:** While Marty's theorem links normality to the boundedness of spherical derivatives, proving that the spherical derivatives of $a_n(k)$ remain bounded *only* on the interior $k \in (k_-, k_+)$ and blow up everywhere on $\partial D$ requires precise uniform bounds on the multinomial coefficients of $a_n(k)$, which grow too rapidly for naive binomial estimates.

By the Mean Value Theorem applied to $f(t, \delta) = -e^{-t\delta}$, the error satisfies $e_{n+1} = e_n - e^{-n\zeta_n} n e_n + r_n$, where $\zeta_n$ lies between $\delta_n$ and $\delta(n)$. Invoking the discrete Gronwall inequality (Bellman's lemma for sequences), if $u_{n+1} \le (1 - \alpha_n) u_n + \beta_n$ with $0 < \alpha_n < 1$, then $u_n \le u_{n_0} \prod_{j=n_0}^{n-1} (1 - \alpha_j) + \sum_{j=n_0}^{n-1} \beta_j \prod_{k=j+1}^{n-1} (1 - \alpha_k)$. Here, the contraction coefficient is $\alpha_n = n e^{-n\zeta_n}$.

3. **Contraction coefficient estimate near the boundary**: For the critical boundary scaling where $\delta_n \sim \frac{2\ln n}{n}$, the contraction coefficient is $\alpha_n \approx n \exp(-n \cdot \frac{2\ln n}{n}) = n \cdot n^{-2} = \frac{1}{n}$. Because $\sum \frac{1}{n} = \infty$ while the infinite product $\prod (1 - \frac{1}{n})$ diverges to $0$, the linear variational system is marginally stable. This confirms that perturbations decay or grow critically depending on the subleading logarithmic corrections identified in `lemma_8`.

4. **Resolution of the logarithmic mismatch via matched asymptotics**: To resolve `obstacle_2`, the remainder $r_n$ in the discrete step must match the difference between the discrete operator $\Delta \delta_n$ and the continuous derivative. Writing $\delta_n = \frac{2\ln n + \ln\ln n + C}{n} + \frac{\gamma_n}{n \ln n}$, the discrete operator $\delta_{n+1} - \delta_n$ matches $-e^{-n\delta_n}$ up to order $O(n^{-2} (\ln n)^{-1})$ precisely when the subleading sequence $\gamma_n$ satisfies a linearized recurrence balancing the $n \delta_n^2$ term against the continuous flow.

## Obstacles

1. **Variable and non-uniform Lipschitz bounds**: The partial derivative $\partial_\delta (-e^{-t\delta}) = t e^{-t\delta}$ varies rapidly with $t$ and $\delta$. When $\delta$ strays from the critical curve $\frac{2\ln t}{t}$, the Lipschitz constant can exceed $1$, violating the standard contraction hypothesis $\alpha_n < 1$ required for naive applications of the discrete Gronwall inequality.
2. **Sharpness of the remainder bounds**: The truncation error contains $n \delta_n^2$. For $\delta_n = \frac{2\ln n + \ln\ln n + C}{n}$, we have $n \delta_n^2 \sim \frac{4(\ln n)^2}{n}$, which decays slower than the spacing between distinct choices of the integration constant $C$. Thus, third- and fourth-order terms in the exponential expansion must be controlled uniformly to prevent spurious drift in the Gronwall bounds.

## Suggested next steps

1. **Formulate the weighted discrete Gronwall lemma**: State and prove a localized version of the discrete Gronwall inequality with variable weights $w_n = \prod_{j=n_0}^{n-1} (1 - c j^{-1} + O(j^{-2}))$ to rigorously absorb the marginal stability when $\alpha_n \sim c/n$.
2. **Compute the explicit third-order remainder**: Expand $(1-\delta_n)^n - e^{-n\delta_n + \frac{n}{2}\delta_n^2 - \frac{n}{3}\delta_n^3}$ explicitly and bound it by $O(n^{-2} (\ln n)^{-3})$ under the assumption $\delta_n \in [0, 2\ln n / n]$.
3. **Match inner and outer asymptotic layers**: Construct a two-term matched asymptotic expansion for $\delta_n$ explicitly separating the bulk behavior from the discrete-to-continuous transition near $n=3$, and use it to fix the constant $C$ in `lemma_8`.

1. **Fatal logarithmic mismatch in the boundary ansatz:** Lemma 8 and Lemma 13 claim the asymptotic form $\delta_n \sim \frac{2 \ln n}{n}$. Substituting this into the discrete difference gives $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} \approx -\frac{d}{dn}\left(\frac{2\ln n}{n}\right) \sim \frac{2\ln n}{n^2}$ (at leading order, ignoring the $-2/n^2$ term). If we include the next term in the ansatz, $\delta_n = \frac{2\ln n + \ln\ln n + C}{n}$, the right-hand side becomes $e^{-n\delta_n} = e^{-C} n^{-2} (\ln n)^{-1} = \frac{e^{-C}}{n^2 \ln n}$. This creates an irreconcilable factor of $(\ln n)^2$ between the left-hand side ($\sim \frac{2\ln n}{n^2}$) and the right-hand side ($\sim \frac{1}{n^2 \ln n}$). The proposed balance fails algebraically.
2. **Unjustified truncation of the logarithmic expansion of $(1-\delta_n)^n$:** The expansion $(1-\delta_n)^n = \exp\left(-n\delta_n - \frac{n}{2}\delta_n^2 - \frac{n}{3}\delta_n^3 - \dots\S\right)$ relies on $\delta_n \to 0$. If $\delta_n \sim \frac{2\ln n}{n}$, then the second term in the exponent is $\frac{n}{2}\delta_n^2 \sim \frac{n}{2} \frac{4(\ln n)^2}{n^2} = \frac{2(\ln n)^2}{n}$. While this vanishes as $n \to \infty$, it decays slower than $1/\ln n$ and shifts the effective argument inside the exponential, meaning higher-order terms in the Taylor expansion of $\ln(1-\delta_n)$ actively couple into the leading-order balance.
3. **Inapplicability of the continuous ODE surrogate (Lemma 13):** The replacement of the finite difference $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1}$ with the continuous derivative $-\dot{\delta}(t)$ via $\dot{x}(t) = x(t)^t$ discards Euler-Maclaurin correction terms. In discrete recursions of the form $x_{n+1} - x_n = f(x_n, n)$, matching continuous flows often misses subtle shifts induced by the discrete lattice step $\Delta n = 1$, which can alter logarithmic prefactors by a factor of 2 or more.

## Obstacles

- The claimed asymptotic rate $\delta_n \sim \frac{2\ln n}{n}$ is algebraically inconsistent with the recurrence relation $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} = (1-\delta_n)^n$; either the prefactor '2' is wrong, or the power of $\ln n$ in the numerator/denominator was miscalculated in the matching process.

## Findings
1. **Lagrange Inversion Theorem for the step map:** Let $f_n(x) = x + x^n$. To invert $w = f_n(x)$ near $x=1$ or near the critical point, we can apply the Lagrange Inversion Theorem (or the Lagrange-Good formula). Expressing the inverse branch $f_n^{-1}(w)$ as a power series in $z = w - w_0$ gives coefficients determined by contour integrals of the form $\frac{1}{k!} \left( \frac{d^{k-1}}{dx^{k-1}} \left( \frac{x}{f_n(x) - w_0} \right)^k \right)\big|_{x=x_0}$. This provides explicit local analytic representations for the inverse branches away from the turning points.
2. **Local asymptotic expansion via the Lambert $W$ function:** Near the boundary where $w \approx 1$, setting $w = 1 - \epsilon$ and $x = 1 - \delta_n$, the local relation is $1 - \epsilon = (1 - \delta_n) + (1 - \delta_n)^n$. Approximating $(1-\delta_n)^n \approx e^{-n \delta_n}$ yields the transcendental equation $\epsilon + \delta_n \approx e^{-n\delta_n}$. The local inverse branch is given explicitly by $\delta_n(\epsilon) \approx -\frac{1}{n} W(-n \epsilon e^n)$ (using the appropriate branch of the Lambert $W$ function), capturing the multi-valued nature and logarithmic singularities near $w=1$.
3. **Puiseux expansions and fold catastrophes:** Near the critical threshold $c^*_n$ where $f_n(x)$ has a local extremum (saddle-node bifurcation), the inversion $f_n(x) = w$ fails to be unicursal. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem or local normal form theory, the inverse branches bifurcate via a Puiseux series in fractional powers of $(w - c^*_n)^{1/2}$, characteristic of a Whitney fold. This explains how open sets are compressed, flattened, and folded across the thin boundary layers.
4. **Stretching of open sets via compositional inverse Jacobians:** The global $n$-th inverse map is a composition $F_n^{-1} = f_2^{-1} \circ f_3^{-1} \circ \dots \circ f_n^{-1}$. The Jacobian of this compositional inverse involves the infinite product of derivatives $\prod_{i=3}^n (1 + i a_i^{i-1})^{-1}$. As $a_i \to 1$, each factor $(1 + i)^{-1}$ or similar causes rapid contraction of distance in the forward direction, which translates to exponential stretching (magnification) of open intervals under $F_n^{-1}$, driving the boundary layer thinning.

## Obstacles
1. **Non-autonomous composition non-commutativity:** Unlike autonomous dynamical systems where one iterates a single function $f^{-1} \circ f^{-1} \circ \dots$, our system composes *different* inverse branches $f_i^{-1}$ at each step $i$. Consequently, standard conjugacy and invariant curve theorems do not apply directly, and branch cuts accumulate in a non-stationary manner.
2. **Stokes line accumulation in the complex plane:** The multi-valued branches of the Lambert $W$ approximation $\delta_n \approx -\frac{1}{n} W(-n \epsilon e^n)$ generate Stokes lines across which the asymptotic expansion transitions abruptly. As $n \to \infty$, these Stokes lines condense densely near the real boundary points $k_+$ and $k_-$, making uniform error bounds extremely difficult to establish.
3. **Breakdown of Lagrange inversion near inflection/critical points:** The standard Lagrange inversion formula assumes non-vanishing derivative $\frac{df_n}{dx} \neq 0$ at the expansion center. Near the critical values $c^*_n$, the derivative vanishes ($1 + n x^{n-1} = 0$), causing the Lagrange series coefficients to diverge due to poles colliding with the contour of integration.

## Suggested next steps
1. **Analyze the multi-sheeted Riemann surface of the compositional inverse:** Construct the composite inverse map $\mathcal{F}_n^{-1}(w) = (f_n^{-1} \circ f_{n-1}^{-1} \circ \dots \circ f_3^{-1})(w)$ numerically and track how the branch cuts of the Lambert $W$ function partition the complex $k$-plane into fundamental domains.
2. **Rigorous saddle-point analysis of the Lagrange integral:** Rewrite the Lagrange inversion coefficients as a contour integral and apply the method of steepest descent to rigorously quantify the transition width of the boundary layer as a function of $n$.
3. **Catastrophe matching across consecutive layers:** Model the transition from the polynomial iterate $a_n$ to the continuous ODE surrogate ($\dot{x} = x^t$) using matched asymptotic expansions, matching the local Puiseux fold coordinates to the outer global trajectory.

payload.content:
## Findings

1. **Non-autonomous function sequence and chain rule:** Let $f_n(z) = z + z^n$ for $n \ge 3$, with $z_3 = z$ and $z_{n+1} = f_n(z_n)$. The total derivative of the $n$-th iterate with respect to the initial parameter $z$ is given by the chain rule as $D_n(z) = \frac{d z_n}{d z} = \prod_{j=3}^{n-1} f_j'(z_j)$, where $f_j'(z) = 1 + j z^{j-1}$.
2. **Candidate non-autonomous Lyapunov exponent:** A natural candidate for the finite-time Lyapunov exponent is $\lambda_n(z) = \frac{1}{n} \ln |D_n(z)| = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=3}^{n-1} \ln |1 + j z_j^{j-1}|$. The asymptotic Lyapunov exponent $\lambda(z) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \lambda_n(z)$ would ostensibly characterize the sensitivity to initial conditions.
3. **Divergence of $\lambda(z)$ at the boundary $z \to 1$:** For initial parameters $z$ on the convergence boundary where $z_n \to 1$ (such as $a_3 = c^*$), we have $z_j \to 1$, which implies $f_j'(z_j) = 1 + j z_j^{j-1} \sim j$. Consequently, the sum $\sum_{j=3}^{n-1} \ln |1 + j z_j^{j-1}|$ behaves as $\sum_{j=3}^{n-1} \ln j \sim n \ln n$. Dividing by $n$ gives $\lambda_n(z) \sim \ln n \to \infty$. 
4. **Rescaled Lyapunov exponent requirement:** Because the degree of the iteration function $f_n(z)$ increases with $n$ ($d_n = n$), the standard normalization factor $1/n$ fails to produce a finite limit on the boundary. A proper non-autonomous Lyapunov exponent for this system must be normalized by the log-factorial growth, i.e., $\tilde{\lambda}_n(z) = \frac{1}{n \ln n} \ln |D_n(z)|$.

## Obstacles

1. **Failure of classical Fatou-Julia theory:** Classical polynomial iteration relies on a constant degree $d \ge 2$, ensuring that the Green's function $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{d^n} \ln^+ |z_n|$ exists. Here, the degree $n$ grows at each step, meaning the invariant potential must be defined with respect to cumulative products of degrees rather than geometric powers.
2. **Singular behavior of $\lambda(z)$ on the boundary:** As shown in finding 3, the naive Lyapunov exponent blows up logarithmically on the boundary $z_n \to 1$ rather than vanishing or remaining bounded. Thus, the zero-level set $\lambda(z) = 0$ does not directly delineate the convergence boundary in the standard way.

## Suggested next steps

1. **Define a modified Green's function:** Construct the potential $\Phi(z) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \prod_{j=3}^n j \right)^{-1/n} \dots$ or use the logarithmic scale $\Psi(z) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\ln |z_n|}{\sum_{j=3}^n \ln j}$ to properly measure the exponential growth rates of orbits when $z_n \to \infty$.
2. **Analyze the rescaled derivative sum:** Prove or disprove that the limit $\tilde{\lambda}(z) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n \ln n} \ln |D_n(z)|$ exists and equals $1$ on the boundary where $z_n \to 1$, and equals $0$ in the interior domain of convergence where $z_n$ converges to a fixed point in $(0, 1)$.

Proper rescaled normalization \tilde{\lambda}_n(z) = \frac{1}{n \ln n} \ln |D_n(z)|$ is required for non-autonomous sensitivity analysis.

payload.task: Investigate the analytic continuation and singular structure of the generating function G(z) = sum delta_n z^n near the natural boundary |z|=1 as described in lemma_17, and explore whether the singularities reflect a Fuchsian-type equation or non-autonomous Julia set boundaries in complex dynamics (referencing question_1).
payload.content:
## Findings

1. **Non-holonomicity and the failure of Fuchsian equations:** A linear ordinary differential equation is Fuchsian if all its singularities (including at infinity) are regular singular points. By a classical theorem of Fuchs, any solution to a Fuchsian ODE has at worst algebraic branching around its singularities, meaning its analytic continuation can only encounter a finite set of isolated singularities. If $|z|=1$ is a *natural boundary* (as claimed in Lemma 17), then the generating function $G(z) = \sum \delta_n z^n$ *cannot* satisfy any linear ODE with algebraic coefficients (i.e., $G(z)$ is not D-finite / holonomic). This rules out any Fuchsian-type or even general linear differential equation framework for $G(z)$ directly.

2. **Subdominant oscillations and Hadamard-type singularity accumulation:** I conjecture that the asymptotic expansion $\delta_n = \frac{2\ln n + c_1\ln\ln n + C}{n}$ misses crucial subdominant oscillatory terms of the form $n^{-1} \cos(b \ln n + \phi)$ arising from the linearization of the discrete map around the continuous ODE flow (Floquet exponents of the saddle point). In Dirichlet and power series, such imaginary frequencies in the exponent generate dense sets of singularities on the circle of convergence via limit points, providing the mechanism for $|z|=1$ to act as a natural boundary in analogy with Hadamard's gap-type theorems.

3. **$q$-Difference and Mellin transform perspective:** Because the exponent in the recurrence is $n$ (reflecting $e^{n \ln a_n}$), the generating function $G(z)$ shares formal structures with $q$-series and Lambert series. Consider the Mellin transform $\mathcal{M}\{\delta_n\}(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \delta_n n^{s-1}$. Translating the recurrence-induced asymptotics into the Mellin domain typically yields meromorphic continuations with strings of poles equally spaced along imaginary lines (e.g., $\operatorname{Re}(s) = 0$ with periodic imaginary offsets). By inverse Mellin transformation, these pole lattices translate precisely into natural boundaries on $|z|=1$ for the associated power series.

4. **Analogy with the inverse Riemann mapping of non-autonomous Julia sets:** As noted in Question 1 and Lemma 10/11, the derivative $L'(k)$ blows up at the boundary $k_+$, and the parameter space exhibits non-autonomous Julia set features (Idea 4). In complex dynamics, the generating function or coordinate change that linearizes a dynamical system often has a natural boundary corresponding exactly to the Julia set (where the invariant measure or Green's function ceases to be harmonic). Thus, the natural boundary of $G(z)$ on $|z|=1$ is the analytic-combinatorial shadow of the non-autonomous Julia set boundary in the complex $k$-plane pulled back via the parameter dependence.

## Obstacles

- **Proving the natural boundary rigorously:** Showing that $|z|=1$ is a natural boundary requires proving that no analytic continuation exists across *any* dense subset of the unit circle. Standard singularity analysis (like Flajolet-Odlyzko transfer theorems) assumes algebraic-logarithmic singularities at isolated points (usually $z=1$), whereas a natural boundary requires proving the circle is a barrier of essential singularities, which is notoriously difficult for nonlinear recurrences without a modular or arithmetic invariance.
- **Controlling the subdominant terms:** The exact transition from the discrete recurrence $\delta_n - \delta_{n+1} = (1-\delta_n)^n$ to the continuous ODE $\dot{\delta} = -e^{-t\delta}$ suppresses discrete phase information. Unless one rigorously bounds the error term $O(n^{-1})$ to show it lacks hidden quasi-periodic oscillations, the claim that $|z|=1$ is a natural boundary remains heuristic.

## Suggested next steps

1. **Compute high-precision Taylor coefficients:** Numerically compute the first 500 terms of $\delta_n$ using multiprecision arithmetic and evaluate the analytic continuation of $G(z)$ outside $|z|=1$ using Padé approximants or Levin sequence transformations to empirically verify whether the singularities form a dense barrier or a natural boundary.
2. **Analyze the Mellin-Barnes integral representation:** Formulate the recurrence for $\delta_n$ as a functional equation for the Dirichlet-type series $D(s) = \sum \delta_n n^{-s}$ and investigate its strip of convergence and pole structure using Mellin transform techniques.
3. **Check for Mahler or $q$-difference functional equations:** Test whether the sequence $\delta_n$ satisfies an approximate $q$-difference relation of the form $F(q z) = P(z, F(z))$ which is known to naturally induce natural boundaries on circles of convergence.
